**Element Layout (14.2 points):**
The split-screen design effectively separates conceptual text from visual proofs. Text is legible against the dark background, though the right-side animations occasionally feel slightly crowded when multiple coordinate systems overlap.

**Attractiveness (13.8 points):**
The minimalist aesthetic and high-contrast color palette are professionally executed. The smooth grid transitions are engaging, though the visual style remains somewhat functional rather than artistically innovative.

**Logic Flow (15.5 points):**
The progression from an intuitive 'perspective' metaphor to formal matrix notation is excellent. Scaffolding is well-handled, moving from definitions to mechanical application and then practical justification.

**Accuracy & Depth (14.8 points):**
The content is mathematically rigorous and factually correct. It successfully bridges the gap between geometric intuition and algebraic representation, providing a clear explanation of why the change of basis matrix functions as a 'translator'.

**Visual Consistency (14.5 points):**
Color coding for specific basis sets and vectors remains uniform throughout the presentation. The transition between static text and dynamic grid warping is seamless, maintaining a coherent design language.

**Overall Summary:**
This is a high-quality instructional video that effectively communicates the 'Change of Basis' concept. It balances intuition with technical accuracy, utilizing a clean, professional visual style to reduce cognitive load while maintaining learner interest.

**Key Strengths:**
• Effective use of the 'Maya and Drone' metaphor for perspective
• Clear color-coding between algebraic symbols and visual elements
• Strong pedagogical scaffolding from simple to complex

**Areas for Improvement:**
• Increase whitespace in the animation panel during complex grid overlaps
• Slightly slower pacing during the introduction of the P-inverse formula
• Enhanced visual distinction between the standard basis and custom basis vectors

B
A basis is defined by two essential properties: its vectors must be linearly independent (no vector can be written as a combination of the others) and they must span the space (any vector in the space can be written as a combination of the basis vectors).

B
Changing the basis re-expresses vectors and transformations in a new coordinate system. This is done to find a representation where the problem is simpler, such as turning a complex matrix into a diagonal one (diagonalization) or aligning the coordinate axes with the geometry of the problem.

B
A vector with coordinates (2, 0) in a basis aligned with it has a magnitude of 2. If this new basis is rotated 45 degrees relative to the standard X-Y basis, the vector's components in the standard basis would be (2*cos(45°), 2*sin(45°)), which calculates to (√2, √2).

B
A change of basis matrix is a square matrix used to transform the coordinates of a vector from an initial basis to a new basis through matrix multiplication.

B
To find the coordinates of a vector in a new basis, you must express that vector as a linear combination of the new basis vectors. The coefficients of this linear combination are the new coordinates.
